data.text: Intro

Jackson Heights, located in the Northwest section of Queens, is a culturally diverse neighborhood in New York City and perhaps in the world. As the New York Times stated, "Jackson Heights is the most culturally diverse neighborhood in New York City and possibly in the entire world". Jackson Heights is home to approximately 108,000 to 175,000 residents, of which 60% to 64% were born outside the United States.

Therefore, Jackson Heights is a true melting pot that speaks more than 167 languages. The majority of the population in Jackson Heights is Hispanic, however, there are also many South Asians, Latin Americans and Himalayan people living there.

data.caption: The Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue/74th Street subway station, gateway to the neighborhood. Photo: Pacific Coast Highway, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

data.text: Yet this vibrant community faces a critical challenge: a severe lack of public open space. Jackson Heights has as little as 2 square feet of park space per resident, ranking last in all New York City neighborhoods. The entire area has fewer than 12 acres of public parks. The lack of public open spaces in Jackson Heights was particularly harmful to the community during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In response, the community created an innovative solution. During the COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020, 34th Avenue was transformed into an Open Street for pedestrians and cyclists. This 1.3 mile stretch spanning 26 blocks, now known as Paseo Park, has been widely recognized as the “gold standard” for New York City’s car‑free open streets. The city has allocated $89 million to make it a permanent linear park. As one community member put it: “There’s nowhere for your children to learn to ride bikes … they don’t have room for recess.” Paseo Park is changing that.
Sources: [1][2][3]

data.caption: Paseo Park (a permanent linear park)

data.text: Jackson Heights is an example of a place with an inclusive street life, as evidenced by events such as the Queens Pride Parade, Momo Crawl and Festival Calle Colombia; these events help ensure that public spaces in Jackson Heights are always active and open to everyone.

data.text: Hard System Overview: Reading Jackson Heights Layer by Layer
This is every hard system layer mapped for Jackson Heights at once: streets, buildings, parks, land use, and transit. Scroll down to see how the neighborhood was built.

data.caption: JH Map0 - Hard System Layers

data.text: The Street Grid

The Queensboro Corporation created a rigid orthogonal grid in 1909 (long blocks ran north-south to maximize sunlight) and mapped out 1,001 street segments ranging from 6 to 70 feet wide, with an average width of 32.6 feet. Traffic is carried on wide arterials, while narrow side streets were constructed for quietness.

Early 19th-century photo, courtesy of Jeffrey A. (The Jackson Heights Garden City Society, Inc.).
JH Map0 - Hard System Layers

data.text: Building Coverage

The Queensboro Corporation deliberately left an opening at the center of each block to create a garden for all residents. The pattern that emerges after removing the streets shows only 30-50% of every block was developed as compared to 90% in similar Manhattan blocks.

data.caption: Building Image from Google Maps
JH Map0 - Hard System Layers

data.text: Open Space

The only thing left are the green areas. All 14 of the interior block gardens that were part of the initial design (15 total) have been converted into private courtyards and therefore are no longer accessible to the general public.

Additionally, there has been an addition of publicly-accessible park space totaling only 14.33 acres which equates to approximately 6.1 square feet per resident.

data.text: Transit
Two subway lines run together along Roosevelt Avenue at the southern edge of the neighborhood: the elevated 7 train (red) and the underground E/F/M/R (blue).
All of the commercial clusters shown on the Land-Use map are located within a short walking distance from either of these lines.

data.caption: JH Map0 - Hard System Layers

data.text: Land Use
In terms of color coding, purple represents retail; blue represents residential; and green represents park or forest.

As expected by the prediction made from the transit layer (red dots), the majority of the neighborhood was residential. Retail areas were located on both sides of the avenues adjacent to the subway stations.

data.caption: JH Map0 - Hard System Layers

data.text: Phase 1
System Origins: Street Grid + Whole-Block Landscape Design (1909–1930s)

The Queensboro Corporation adapted the Garden City ideal — originally designed for curving suburban lanes — onto the city's rigid orthogonal grid. Each block was treated as a single landscape unit: a continuous grass strip ran between curb and sidewalk, buildings were set back to create front yards, and the center of every block held a large interior garden. Only about 30–50% of each block was covered by buildings, versus roughly 90% coverage on comparable Manhattan blocks of the same era.

The hard-system variables that define this phase: grid orientation (long blocks run north–south to maximize sunlight), building coverage ratio, courtyard area, and building setback. Notably, Garden City on Long Island used curving roads for the same ideal — Jackson Heights' choice to keep the orthogonal grid was itself a defining hard-system decision.

data.caption: A typical residential street in Jackson Heights, showing the front-yard setbacks and street trees of the original plan. Photo: Jleon, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons.

data.text: Sources: [4][5][6]

data.caption: Map 1 — Street & open-space cross-section: building footprints (brown), interior block gardens (green), and the street grid. Note how coverage varies block by block.

data.text: Zooming In: One Block Cluster

The full-neighborhood maps above compress a lot of information. Here we zoom into one representative cluster of blocks near Broadway and Roosevelt Avenue, close enough to read individual buildings, gardens, and streets. Two features are marked below.

data.caption: JH Map1 - Street & Open Space Profile

data.text: The Interior Block Garden

The green shapes here are not backyards — they are shared interior gardens, the defining feature of the 1909 plan. The T-shaped building on the right wraps around its own courtyard; the block to its left holds a single large garden shared by every surrounding building. Click the marked point to read more.

data.caption: JH Map1 - Street & Open Space Profile

data.text: Broadway: Breaking the Grid

Almost every street in this cluster runs at a strict right angle, except one. Broadway cuts diagonally across the top of this view, a route that predates the 1909 plan. The Queensboro Corporation could not erase it, so the grid simply bends around it, producing the handful of irregular, triangular lots visible along its edge.

data.caption: JH Map1 - Street & Open Space Profile

data.text: Measuring the Street: Width and the Public Right-of-Way

The NYC LION street-centerline dataset records an official mapped width for every block face, letting the "continuous grass strip" of the original plan be measured rather than just described. Across Jackson Heights' 1,001 mapped street segments, widths range from 6 to 70 feet, averaging 32.6 feet — with the widest belonging to arterial avenues like Northern Boulevard and 34th Avenue, and the narrowest to the quiet residential side streets the Garden City plan was built around. This variation in the public right-of-way is itself a hard-system fingerprint of the 1909 plan: wide enough for a planted median on the boulevards, narrow enough on side streets to keep traffic subordinate to the block's interior garden.

data.caption: Map 4 — Street width by segment (NYC LION): darker blue = wider right-of-way. Arterial avenues stand out from the narrower residential grid, a direct trace of the 1909 cross-section design.

data.text: 1,001 Segments, One Pattern

Every blue line here is one mapped street segment, colored by width. Zoom in and the pattern from the text above becomes visible on the ground: wide arterial avenues cut diagonally or run at the neighborhood's edges, while the interior grid stays narrow and residential. Two segments are marked below.

data.caption: JH Map4 - Street Width & Cross-Section

data.text: The Widest Right-of-Way

The marked segment on Astoria Boulevard carries the widest mapped right-of-way in the neighborhood — up to 70 feet curb to curb, wide enough for the planted median that runs down its center. It is one of only a handful of arterial-scale streets the 1909 plan had to build its residential grid around.

data.caption: JH Map4 - Street Width & Cross-Section

data.text: The Narrowest Block Faces

Away from the avenues, the grid narrows sharply. These quiet residential streets map to as little as 6 feet of right-of-way — far less traffic capacity than they'd ever need, since the block's real public space was always meant to be the interior garden, not the street. A marked segment nearby carries this story's lowest recorded width.

data.caption: JH Map4 - Street Width & Cross-Section

data.text: Phase 2
From Public Open Space to Privatized Courtyards (1930s–2000)

As the area developed over time, the neighborhood’s first community gardens, tennis courts, and golf course were replaced with new construction. 14 of the 15 original interior block gardens that had been included in the initial design remain today; however, each garden is currently owned and maintained by a private cooperative and therefore cannot be accessed by the general public. This change represents a significant reduction in publicly accessible open space as it changed from an equal combination of public and private open space to virtually all private.
Sources: [4][6][9]

data.caption: Map 2 — Current open space: green = named public parks/playgrounds; orange = unnamed interior-block plots, likely private courtyards (ownership not verified in this dataset).

data.text: Public vs. Private Green
Green areas on this map do not represent the same type of land.

Parcels shown in green are publicly owned parks and playgrounds, maintained by the city and open to anyone. Parcels shown in orange appear as open space in the parcel data but sit inside residential blocks, and the data does not record who owns them or who may enter.

data.caption: JH Map2 - Current Open Space Distribution

data.text: Behind the Buildings
This orange plot sits entirely inside a residential block, invisible from the street.

Existing open data do not establish its ownership or public accessibility. Given the co-op history of Jackson Heights, the most plausible interpretation is a private garden maintained by and reserved for residents of the surrounding buildings.

data.caption: The interior garden from Google Maps
JH Map2 - Current Open Space Distribution

data.text: A Genuinely Public Park
The green parcel on this map is a designated park: officially named, city-owned, open to anyone who walks in.
It sits a block from the orange courtyard on the previous slide. In the data, the two are indistinguishable. On the ground, one has an entrance and the other has a door.

data.caption: A public park from Google Maps

data.text: Phase 3
System Stress and Rebalancing (2000–Present)

By the 2000s, population growth and the formation of a dense immigrant community, in which more than 60% of residents were foreign-born, came into direct conflict with the shortage of public open space produced by Phase 2. Jackson Heights' open space ratio (OSR) is 0.91, compared with a Queens-wide average of 3.37. The 34th Avenue Open Street, now called Paseo Park, is a direct outcome of that tension. During the pandemic, 1.3 miles and 26 blocks of roadway were converted into a linear park, when the neighborhood was described as "the epicenter of the epicenter." Only seven blocks are fully pedestrianized, however; the remainder operate as shared streets where vehicles are permitted at 5 mph. The roughly 7-acre footprint therefore measures roadway reallocated, not open space acquired. The contemporary hard-system variables are OSR, the footprint of Paseo Park (about 7 acres), and schoolyard-to-park conversions such as PS 69.

data.caption: Paseo Park from Google Maps

data.text: In Jackson Heights, approximately 25 acres of mapped park and open-space parcels consist of 14.33 acres across 15 named, confirmed-public parks and playgrounds, as well as an additional 10.35 acres of interior-block parcels which are probably private cooperative courtyards (refer to Map 2). Compared to the neighborhood's 2020 census population of 101,848 (according to NYC Planning Population FactFinder), the confirmed-public park total equals approximately 6.1 square feet of park space per resident, and an open-space ratio close to 1.4 acres of park space per 10,000 residents — a parcel-based estimation that matches the borough-wide park deficit reported by NYC Planning and Trust for Public Land above.

data.caption: Map 3 — Paseo Park (magenta line, 34th Avenue) runs through the heart of the neighborhood, flanked by public schools (blue triangles) and connected to the subway network (dark squares) — illustrating why this corridor became the pressure valve for the open-space shortfall.

data.text: A Corridor, Not Just a Line

Paseo Park isn't an island; it works within the rest of the neighborhood. The schools (the blue triangles) and the subway stop are connected to each side of the park, and everything is part of the larger transportation system. The two connections can be seen below.

data.text: School on the Open Street

The school marked on the map fronts onto one of Paseo Park's car-free plaza blocks — one of five placed in front of every public school along the corridor. Removing traffic from arrival and dismissal is why parents and school staff were among the project's strongest supporters.

Paseo Park runs three blocks north of Roosevelt Avenue, putting the 7, E, F, M, and R trains within a five-minute walk at multiple points along the corridor. The park is not an isolated amenity but part of the daily commute.

data.text: Contemporary Street Transformation: Bike Infrastructure and Green Stormwater Systems

data.caption: The "Paseo Park" street sign at 79th Street, marking the former traffic lane now reserved for pedestrians and cyclists. Photo: Kidfly182, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

data.text: The right-of-way was fixed in 1909. Everything since has been layered onto it rather than added to it.
Two Retrofits, One Grid

Two contemporary layers sit on top of the 1909 street grid: a bike network classified by protection level, and hundreds of green-infrastructure assets (bioswales, tree pits, stormwater greening) installed along the curb. The next two slides isolate each one.
Layer 1: The Bike Network

Nearly the entire bicycle network in Jackson Heights is Class II — a painted stripe within the roadway, offering no physical barrier between cyclists and moving traffic (red). A single short Class I segment, physically separated from traffic, appears in the entire study area (purple). The remainder consists of scattered Class III treatments — shared lanes marked only with sharrows and signage, where cyclists ride in the traffic lane itself (green) — and one corridor combining Class II and III (blue). Most of the grid carries no bicycle facility at all.

data.caption: A protected, planter-buffered bike lane in New York City — the same design standard NYC DOT applies to Class I segments citywide. Photo: Jim.henderson, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

data.text: Layer 2: Green Infrastructure

Hundreds of green-infrastructure assets — bioswales and stormwater greenstreets installed along the curb by NYC DEP — appear across the neighborhood. Unlike the bike network, they do not concentrate on a few arterials. They spread block by block across the entire grid, reaching the narrow Phase 1 side streets that carry no bicycle facility at all.

data.caption: Map 5. Bicycle network and green infrastructure, Jackson Heights. Purple — Class I (separated); red — Class II (painted); green — Class III (sharrow); blue — II/III combined; grey — none. Orange points — green-infrastructure assets. Source: NYC LION, bike_lane codes 1/2/3/6.

data.text: Shaping Jackson Heights
"The city shapes the community. The community reshapes the city."

In 1909, the Queensboro Corporation imposed a Garden City ideal onto a rigid grid, engineering generous open space into every block. Over the following century, that engineered generosity was steadily enclosed, first by private co-ops and later by mounting population pressure, until the neighborhood with the least park space per resident in New York City had to invent its own: a street. Paseo Park is not a planner's amenity handed down from above; it is what residents built when the system stopped providing. Planned for a community. Reshaped by the people.
When One System Becomes the Other
Three phases in this storymap show the two systems trading places rather than merely coming into contact.

• Paseo Park. Street width — a hard-system asset — now functions as the neighborhood's largest open space, without being mapped as parkland and without a single change to the underlying geometry. The asphalt did not move; its assignment did.
  • The interior block gardens. Technically private open space, each is reachable only through a driveway cut into the street wall. The street system decides who enters the open-space system.
  • The bioswales. They sit inside the street right-of-way but do a park's work: absorbing stormwater, carrying tree canopy. Parkland function, street-system land.
The boundary the Garden City planners drew in 1909 has proven porous. Jackson Heights keeps resolving a shortage in one system by quietly converting capacity from the other.
